newsitem.title: USA: Maxim files IND for trial of Maxamine.
newsitem.headline: Maxim files IND for trial of Maxamine.

text.p: Maxim Pharmaceuticals Inc said Monday that it filed an Investigational New Drug application with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to conduct a phase III clinical trial of its lead compound, Maxamine, to treat malignant melanoma. The company's goal is to begin the clinical trial and initiate patient enrollment during the second quarter of 1997.

The planned phase III study will be a multi-center, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 10 to 12 U.S. centers and possibly include one to two foreign sites. The company anticipates recruiting at least 125 patients with advanced (stage IV) malignant melanoma. The study is intended to demonstrate the safety and efficacy of Maxamine with the following planned primary endpoints: time to disease progression; tumor response; duration of response; and overall patient survival. The estimated duration of the trial is about 12 months once patient enrollment is complete.

In this study, Maxamine will be coadministered with the cytokine, Interleukin-2 (IL-2). In previous clinical studies, study groups treated with Maxamine have demonstrated survival duration to a mean of over 15 months, compared to an mean of 7 months with existing treatments. This increase in survival duration was achieved even when low doses of cytokines were coadministered with Maxamine.

Using the low cytokine doses reduced their side-effects and facilitated self-administration of the drugs at home. According to the American Cancer Society, melanoma is one of the fastest growing cancers with about 130,000 Americans currently afflicted with this disease.

In addition to the phase II trials conducted to date with malignant melanoma patients, Maxamine has also been tested in individuals suffering from acute myelogenous leukemia. Earlier stage clinical trials are ongoing for other cancer indications.

Maxamine, designed as a combination therapy to strengthen and assist the activity of cytokines, may provide more effective therapy for treating certain cancers and infectious diseases. The company's investigators have described an interaction between phagocytes, a type of white blood cell, and NK-cells which may explain the generally low efficacy rates of cytokines in humans. Specific signals transmitted by phagocytes cause NK-cells to initiate apoptosis (programmed cell death) thereby destroying their cytotoxic (anti-tumor) capability. The administration of cytokines, regardless of the dosage, cannot reverse apoptosis.
